category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: A neonate presents with a unilateral cleft of the upper lip. This defect is caused by the failure of the [___] prominence to fuse with the medial nasal prominence.
back: maxillary

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Explain the origin and components of the intermaxillary segment.
back:
• Formed by the deep merging of the two medial nasal prominences.
• Labial component: Philtrum of the upper lip.
• Jaw component: Carries four incisor teeth.
• Palatal component: Forms the triangular primary palate.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Contrast the embryological failures leading to a lateral cleft lip versus an oblique facial cleft.
back:
• Lateral Cleft Lip: Maxillary prominence fails to fuse with the medial nasal prominence.
• Oblique Facial Cleft: Maxillary prominence fails to fuse with the lateral nasal prominence, exposing the nasolacrimal duct.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Identify the embryonic structures that fuse to form the lower lip and jaw.
back:
• Mandibular prominences (paired).
• These arise from the first pharyngeal arch and merge across the midline.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: A rare midline (median) cleft lip results from the incomplete merging of the [___] in the midline.
back: medial nasal prominences

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: An infant presents with bilateral pits in the lower lip and a cleft palate. Identify the most likely genetic syndrome and the mutated gene.
back:
• Van der Woude syndrome.
• IRF6 (Interferon Regulatory Factor 6) gene mutation.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Discuss the clinical significance of a median cleft lip regarding brain development.
back:
• Suggests a significant deficiency of midline tissue.
• High association with holoprosencephaly (loss of midline forebrain structures).
• Often linked to SHH signaling mutations or teratogens like alcohol.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Compare the gender-based prevalence of cleft lip (with or without palate) versus isolated cleft palate.
back:
• Cleft Lip (+/- Palate): More frequent in males (approx. 65%).
• Isolated Cleft Palate: More frequent in females (approx. 55%).

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Name the specific landmark that divides anterior cleft deformities from posterior cleft deformities.
back:
• Incisive foramen.
• Anterior: Cleft lip, primary palate.
• Posterior: Secondary palate, uvula.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: The eyes begin development as a pair of lateral outpocketings from the [___] during the fourth week of gestation.
back:
• Prosencephalon (Forebrain)
• Forms the optic vesicles
• Induced to develop by contact with surface ectoderm

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: A neonate presents with a keyhole-shaped defect in the inferior iris. This condition, known as coloboma, results from the failed closure of the [___].
back:
• Choroid (retinal) fissure
• Normal closure occurs during the 7th week
• Can extend to involve the ciliary body or retina

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Explain how the optic vesicle facilitates the formation of the lens during early eye development.
back:
• Vesicle contacts surface ectoderm
• Induces ectodermal thickening (lens placode)
• Placode invaginates to form the lens vesicle

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Contrast the embryological fate and histological characteristics of the outer versus inner layers of the optic cup.
back:
• Outer: Becomes the pigmented layer of the retina
• Inner: Becomes the neural retina (rods, cones, bipolar cells)
• Space: Separated by the intraretinal space until fusion

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Identify the master regulatory gene for eye development and describe its expression pattern in the early eye field.
back:
• PAX6
• Initially expressed in a single band in the anterior neural ridge
• Later restricted to the optic cup and lens

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: During fetal life, the [___] artery supplies the lens and inner eye before degenerating to leave the central artery of the retina.
back:
• Hyaloid artery
• Located within the choroid fissure
• Distal portion disappears; proximal portion persists

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: An infant is born with a single midline eye (cyclopia) and fused cerebral hemispheres. This defect is primarily linked to a deficiency in which signaling molecule?
back:
• Sonic Hedgehog (SHH)
• Required for dividing the single eye field
• Upregulates PAX2 at the midline

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Describe the structural transformation that occurs as the optic stalk becomes the definitive optic nerve.
back:
• Ganglion cell axons enter the stalk
• Choroid fissure closes around hyaloid vessels
• Stalk walls fuse to enclose the nerve fibers

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Distinguish between the pars optica retinae and pars ceca retinae regarding their location and differentiation.
back:
• Pars optica: Posterior 4/5ths; forms photoreceptive neural layers
• Pars ceca: Anterior 1/5th; forms iris and ciliary body layers
• Transition: Junction occurs at the future ora serrata

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Name the specific transcription factor that is upregulated in the optic stalk to promote its differentiation and separate it from the optic cup.
back:
• PAX2
• Differentiates the stalk from the PAX6-positive cup
• Crucial for choroid fissure formation

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
coreConcept: Embryological Origin of the Optic Vesicle
front: The optic vesicle originates as a lateral outgrowth from the [___] during the fourth week of embryonic development.
back:
The **prosencephalon** (forebrain).
* It contacts surface ectoderm to induce lens formation.
* Eventually invaginates to form the double-walled optic cup.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: A newborn presents with a keyhole-shaped defect in the inferior iris. This condition, coloboma, results from the failed closure of the [___].
back:
**Choroid fissure** (optic fissure).
* Normally closes during the seventh week.
* Defect may extend into the ciliary body, retina, or optic nerve.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Explain the role of the optic vesicle in initiating lens development upon contact with surface ectoderm.
back:
* It acts as an **inducer**.
* Signals (including PAX6) cause ectodermal cells to elongate and thicken.
* This leads to the formation of the **lens placode**, which later invaginates.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Contrast the developmental derivatives of the outer and inner layers of the optic cup.
back:
* **Outer layer:** Becomes the thin, pigmented layer of the retina.
* **Inner layer:** Becomes the thick neural (sensory) retina (rods, cones, and ganglion cells).
* Initially separated by the intraretinal space.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Identify the master regulatory gene responsible for establishing the eye field in the anterior neural plate.
back:
**PAX6**.
* Expressed initially in a single band.
* Later restricted to the optic cup and lens following midline inhibition.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: In early eye development, the signaling molecule [___] is responsible for dividing the single eye field into two separate optic primordia.
back:
**Sonic Hedgehog (SHH)**.
* Secreted by the prechordal plate.
* Upregulates PAX2 in the midline while downregulating PAX6.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: A neonate is born with a single midline eye (cyclopia) and holoprosencephaly. Describe the embryological basis of this presentation.
back:
* Result of **loss of midline tissue**.
* Specifically due to defective SHH signaling.
* Prevents the separation of the initial eye field into bilateral vesicles.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Describe the physiological fate of the intraretinal space during the maturation of the optic cup.
back:
* It is the lumen between the inner and outer cup layers.
* It **obliterates** as the two layers appose.
* It remains a potential site for adult pathological retinal detachment.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Distinguish the pars optica retinae from the pars ceca retinae based on their adult derivatives.
back:
* **Pars optica:** Posterior 4/5; contains photoreceptors (rods/cones).
* **Pars ceca:** Anterior 1/5; forms the inner layers of the iris and ciliary body.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Identify the fetal vascular structure that enters the eye through the choroid fissure to supply the developing lens.
back:
**Hyaloid artery**.
* Distal portion normally degenerates before birth.
* Proximal portion persists as the central artery of the retina.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: The [___] of the upper lip is the central labial component derived from the deeper fusion of the two medial nasal prominences.
back:
Philtrum
* Derived from the intermaxillary segment.
* Formed by the merging of medial nasal prominences.
* Represents the midline portion of the upper lip.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: A newborn presents with a unilateral cleft in the upper lip extending towards the nostril. This defect results from the failure of which two prominences to fuse?
back:
Maxillary and Medial Nasal Prominences
* Caused by failure of mesenchymal bridge formation.
* Occurs on one or both sides (unilateral/bilateral).
* The landmark for classification is the incisive foramen.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Explain the role of the four specific mesenchymal prominences that contribute to the definitive formation of the upper lip.
back:
Upper Lip Composition:
* Two Medial Nasal Prominences: Form the central philtrum.
* Two Maxillary Prominences: Form the lateral parts of the lip.
* Note: Lateral nasal prominences do not participate in lip formation.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Contrast the embryological failures responsible for a typical lateral cleft lip versus the rare median (midline) cleft lip.
back:
Cleft Etiology:
* Lateral Cleft: Failure of maxillary and medial nasal prominences to fuse.
* Median Cleft: Failure of the two medial nasal prominences to merge.
* Clinical Note: Median cleft is often associated with holoprosencephaly.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Identify the adult structures derived from the lateral nasal prominences and specify their involvement in upper lip development.
back:
Lateral Nasal Prominences:
* Derivatives: Form the alae (sides) of the nose.
* Lip Involvement: They contribute zero tissue to the definitive upper lip.
* Separated from maxillary prominences by the nasolacrimal groove.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: During facial development, the [___] groove separates the maxillary prominence from the lateral nasal prominence before canalizing into a duct.
back:
Nasolacrimal
* Ectoderm in the floor of this groove forms a solid cord.
* Detaches and canalizes to form the nasolacrimal duct.
* Upper end widens to form the lacrimal sac.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: An infant presents with a cleft extending from the medial corner of the eye to the upper lip, exposing the nasolacrimal duct. Name the embryological basis.
back:
Oblique Facial Cleft
* Failure of the maxillary prominence to merge with the lateral nasal prominence.
* Results in an exposed nasolacrimal duct.
* Occurs along the line of the nasolacrimal groove.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Describe the three distinct components of the intermaxillary segment formed by the merging of the medial nasal prominences.
back:
Intermaxillary Segment:
* Labial: Forms the philtrum of the upper lip.
* Upper Jaw: Houses the four incisor teeth.
* Palatal: Forms the triangular primary palate.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Distinguish the embryological origins of the upper lip from those of the lower lip.
back:
Lip Origins:
* Upper Lip: Fusion of medial nasal and maxillary prominences.
* Lower Lip: Merging of the two mandibular prominences across the midline.
* Mandibular prominences are the first to merge.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Identify the only unpaired mesenchymal prominence involved in the initial stages of facial development.
back:
Frontonasal Prominence
* Formed by mesenchyme ventral to brain vesicles.
* Gives rise to the forehead and bridge of the nose.
* All other facial prominences (maxillary, mandibular, nasal) are paired.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: The master regulatory gene for eye development, which is initially expressed in a single band in the anterior neural ridge, is [___].
back: • PAX6. • It belongs to the paired box family of transcription factors. • Essential for inducing the eye field and subsequent lens development.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: A neonate presents with a keyhole-shaped defect in the inferior iris. This condition, known as coloboma, results from the failed closure of the [___].
back: • Choroid fissure (also called optic fissure). • Occurs during the seventh week of development. • May extend to the ciliary body, retina, or optic nerve.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Explain the role of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) in the initial patterning of the eye field.
back: • Secreted by the prechordal plate. • Splits the single eye field into two optic primordia. • Suppresses PAX6 in the midline while upregulating PAX2 in the optic stalks.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Contrast the inductive signals required for the differentiation of the neural retina versus the pigmented retinal layer.
back: • Neural Retina: Induced by Fibroblast Growth Factors (FGFs) from the surface ectoderm. • Pigmented Layer: Induced by Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGF-β) from the surrounding mesenchyme.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Identify the unique embryonic source of the sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles.
back: • Derived from the neuroectoderm of the optic cup. • These are rare examples of muscles originating from ectoderm rather than mesoderm.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: During early ocular development, the [___] artery provides the vascular supply to the lens and inner retina before its distal part regresses.
back: • Hyaloid artery. • Enters via the choroid fissure. • The proximal portion persists as the central artery of the retina.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: A newborn presents with fused eyes (synophthalmia) and holoprosencephaly. Describe the embryological basis of this presentation.
back: • Loss of midline tissue during early neurulation (days 19–21). • Failure of the single eye field to separate into two. • Often linked to SHH signaling defects or maternal alcohol exposure.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Describe the anatomical transformation of the optic stalk into the optic nerve.
back: • Retinal axons grow into the stalk's inner wall. • The choroid fissure closes around the hyaloid vessels. • Stalk walls fuse, and neuroglial cells support the expanding nerve fiber bundle.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Distinguish between the pars optica retinae and the pars ceca retinae.
back: • Pars Optica: Posterior 4/5ths of the inner optic cup; contains photoreceptive rods and cones. • Pars Ceca: Anterior 1/5th; remains non-nervous, forming the inner iris and ciliary body layers.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Name the temporary space within the optic cup that disappears as the neural and pigmented layers of the retina appose.
back: • Intraretinal space. • Represents the original lumen of the optic vesicle. • Failure of layer fusion here can lead to congenital retinal detachment.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
coreConcept: Embryological Components of the Upper Lip
front: The upper lip is formed by the fusion of the two [___] nasal prominences and the two [___] prominences.
back: - Medial nasal prominences - Maxillary prominences - Note: The lateral nasal prominences form the alae of the nose but do not contribute to the lip.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: A neonate presents with a facial cleft extending from the medial corner of the eye down to the upper lip, leaving the nasolacrimal duct exposed. Identify the malformation.
back: - Oblique facial cleft - Pathophysiology: Failure of the maxillary prominence to merge with the lateral nasal prominence along the nasolacrimal groove.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Explain the role of the intermaxillary segment in the development of the upper lip's surface anatomy.
back: - It forms the philtrum via its labial component - Derived from the merged medial nasal prominences - It also provides the primary palate and the four incisor teeth.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: A neonate is born with a cleft extending through the upper jaw specifically between the lateral incisor and canine teeth. Analyze which prominences failed to fuse to create this defect.
back: - Maxillary and medial nasal prominences - This location marks the junction of the primary and secondary palate - It is an anterior cleft relative to the incisive foramen.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Identify the mesenchymal prominences that fail to fuse in a standard unilateral lateral cleft lip.
back: - One maxillary prominence and the corresponding medial nasal prominence - This occurs when the maxillary prominence fails to grow medially and compress the medial nasal prominence toward the midline.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: The [___] nasal prominences do not participate in the formation of the upper lip, instead forming the alae (sides) of the nose.
back: - Lateral nasal prominences - These are initially separated from the maxillary prominences by the nasolacrimal groove before merging.

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: A child presents with a rare midline cleft of the upper lip and hypotelorism. Discuss the developmental mechanism and the likely associated neurological defect.
back: - Mechanism: Failure of the two medial nasal prominences to merge due to mesenchymal deficiency - Neurological defect: Holoprosencephaly (merged cerebral ventricles due to loss of midline forebrain tissue).

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Compare the embryological failures leading to a macrostomia (transverse facial cleft) versus a standard lateral cleft lip.
back: - Macrostomia: Failure of fusion between the maxillary and mandibular processes (lateral mouth) - Lateral Cleft: Failure of fusion between the maxillary and medial nasal prominences (upper lip).

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: Distinguish between 'Anterior' and 'Posterior' cleft deformities using the primary anatomical landmark of the palate.
back: - Landmark: Incisive foramen - Anterior: Lateral cleft lip, cleft upper jaw (pre-foramen) - Posterior: Cleft secondary palate and cleft uvula (post-foramen).

category: Describe the development of lip and their associated congenital malformations
front: State the embryological origin of the lower lip and jaw.
back: - Derived from the two mandibular prominences - These originate from the first pharyngeal arch and merge across the midline during the fourth week.

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: The initial development of the eye begins at approximately 22 days as a pair of shallow grooves on the sides of the [___].
back:
• Forebrain (Diencephalon)
• Forms optic vesicles upon closure of the neural tube
• Induces surface ectoderm to form the lens placode

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: A neonate presents with a keyhole-shaped defect in the inferior portion of the iris. This condition results from the failure of the [___] to close during the seventh week of development.
back:
• Choroid Fissure (Optic Fissure)
• Normally allows the hyaloid artery to reach the inner chamber
• Defect may also involve the ciliary body, retina, or optic nerve

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Explain the role of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) in the initial patterning of the eye fields.
back:
• Secreted by the prechordal plate
• Upregulates PAX2 in the midline and optic stalks
• Downregulates PAX6 in the midline to split the single eye field into two

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Contrast the molecular signaling required for the differentiation of the inner neural layer versus the outer pigmented layer of the optic cup.
back:
• Neural layer: Induced by Fibroblast Growth Factors (FGFs) from surface ectoderm
• Pigmented layer: Induced by Transforming Growth Factor-B (TGF-B) from surrounding mesenchyme
• Specific markers: CHX10 (neural) vs. MITF (pigmented)

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Identify the derivatives of the anterior one-fifth of the inner optic cup layer, known as the pars ceca retinae.
back:
• Pars iridica retinae (forms the inner layer of the iris)
• Pars ciliaris retinae (contributes to the ciliary body)
• Remains a single cell layer thick unlike the posterior pars optica

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: During the transformation of the optic stalk into the optic nerve, the hyaloid artery is renamed the [___].
back:
• Central artery of the retina
• Distal portion (supplying the lens) normally degenerates
• Proximal portion remains within the optic nerve core

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: A newborn is found to have a single midline eye (cyclopia) and a proboscis. This spectrum of defects is most closely associated with the loss of midline tissue and a failure of [___].
back:
• Holoprosencephaly
• Caused by failure of the eye field to separate
• Linked to mutations in SHH signaling or maternal alcohol exposure

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Describe the anatomical fate of the intraretinal space during the development of the definitive retina.
back:
• Initially separates the inner neural and outer pigmented layers
• Space is obliterated as the two layers appose each other
• Persistence as a potential space makes it a site for retinal detachment

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Distinguish between the photoreceptive cells of the pars optica retinae based on their sensitivity and function.
back:
• Rods: 120 million; high sensitivity; used for low-light vision; no color detection
• Cones: 6–7 million; lower sensitivity; primary detectors of color
• Both differentiate from the mantle layer bordering the intraretinal space

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Specify the 'master gene' for eye development and its initial expression site in the neural plate.
back:
• PAX6
• Expressed in a band across the anterior neural ridge/eye field
• Essential for lens induction and optic cup formation

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: The initial development of the eye begins as outpocketings of the [___] at approximately 22 days of gestation.
back:
• Forebrain (Diencephalon)
• These outpocketings are called optic grooves
• They expand to form optic vesicles which contact surface ectoderm to induce lens formation

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: A newborn presents with a keyhole-shaped defect in the inferior iris (coloboma). This condition results from the failure of the [___] to close during the seventh week.
back:
• Choroid Fissure (Optic Fissure)
• Failure prevents complete closure of the optic cup and stalk
• May extend to involve the ciliary body, retina, or optic nerve

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Explain how the single eye field in the neural plate is separated into two distinct optic primordia.
back:
• Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) from the prechordal plate inhibits PAX6 in the midline
• SHH upregulates PAX2 in the center to form optic stalks
• This restricts PAX6 expression to the lateral optic cups

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: A neonate is born with a single median eye (cyclopia) and holoprosencephaly. Contrast this pathology with normal eye field separation regarding midline tissue.
back:
• Pathology: Loss of midline tissue prevents eye field separation
• Normal: SHH separates fields; PAX2 forms stalks
• Result: Fusion of optic primordia and cerebral hemispheres into a single vesicle

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Identify the master regulatory gene for eye development and its primary role in the surface ectoderm.
back:
• PAX6
• Essential for lens placode induction
• Upregulates transcription factors SOX2 and LMAF to initiate lens crystallin formation and cell proliferation

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: The [___] space, which initially separates the two layers of the optic cup, eventually disappears as the layers appose each other.
back:
• Intraretinal space
• Represents the lumen of the original optic vesicle
• Clinical link: Weak attachment here is the site of adult retinal detachment

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: A 2-week-old infant is diagnosed with congenital cataracts. This opacity of the lens is often linked to maternal infection with [___] during the 4th to 7th weeks of pregnancy.
back:
• Rubella virus (German measles)
• The lens is vulnerable to the virus before the seventh week
• Later infections typically cause hearing loss rather than cataracts

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Describe the epithelial-mesenchymal interaction required for the differentiation of the neural retina versus the pigmented retina.
back:
• FGFs from surface ectoderm promote neural retina (inner layer)
• TGF-beta from surrounding mesenchyme promotes pigmented retina (outer layer)
• Involves regionalized downstream expression of CHX10 and MITF respectively

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Distinguish the pars optica retinae from the pars ceca retinae based on their adult derivatives.
back:
• Pars Optica: Posterior 4/5ths; contains photoreceptors (rods and cones)
• Pars Ceca: Anterior 1/5th; forms the inner iris and ciliary body layers
• Boundary: Ora serrata

category: Describe the development of optic vesicle and retina
front: Name the vascular structure that reaches the inner chamber of the eye via the choroid fissure and its adult remnant.
back:
• Hyaloid Artery
• Adult Remnant: Central artery of the retina
• The distal portion normally degenerates, leaving the hyaloid canal in the vitreous body

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: The [___] is the specialized thickening of surface ectoderm that invaginates under the inductive influence of the optic vesicle to initiate lens development.
back: Lens placode

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: A neonate presents with a keyhole-shaped defect in the inferior quadrant of the iris. This condition likely resulted from the failure of the [___] to fuse during the 7th week of development.
back: Choroid fissure (Optic fissure)

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Explain the unique embryological origin of the sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles compared to the majority of the body's musculature.
back: They are derived from the **neuroectoderm** of the optic cup, unlike most muscles which originate from mesoderm.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the embryological derivation and histological nature of the choroid versus the sclera.
back: Both arise from mesenchyme; the **Choroid** is the vascular inner layer (pia mater equivalent), while the **Sclera** is the fibrous outer layer (dura mater equivalent).

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Identify the three embryological layers that contribute to the adult structure of the cornea.
back:
1. Surface ectoderm (epithelium).
2. Mesenchyme (stroma/substantia propria).
3. Mesenchymal cells (endothelium).

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: The master regulatory gene that establishes the eye field and is essential for the development of the iris, often mutated in cases of aniridia, is [___].
back: PAX6

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: A child is born with bilateral opaque lenses. The mother reports a rash and fever during the first trimester. Identify the likely environmental trigger and the embryological structure affected.
back:
Trigger: Rubella virus (German measles).
Structure: Lens (Congenital Cataract).

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Describe the mechanism by which the lumen of the lens vesicle is obliterated during the 7th week of gestation.
back: Cells of the **posterior wall** of the lens vesicle elongate anteriorly to form **primary lens fibers**, which gradually fill the vesicle cavity.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Distinguish between the embryological origins of the ciliary muscle and the ciliary processes.
back: The **ciliary muscle** develops from the surrounding mesenchyme, whereas the **ciliary processes** develop from the folding of the pars ciliaris retinae (optic cup ectoderm).

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Identify the embryological basis for the formation of the anterior chamber of the eye.
back: It forms through **vacuolization** of the mesenchyme located between the surface ectoderm and the developing lens.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: The lens of the eye develops from a localized thickening of the surface ectoderm known as the [___].
back:
• Lens placode.
• It invaginates to form the lens vesicle during the 5th week.
• Induces the underlying optic vesicle to invaginate into the optic cup.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: A neonate presents with a keyhole-shaped defect in the inferior iris. This clinical finding results from the failure of the [___] to close.
back:
• Choroid fissure (Optic fissure).
• Normal closure occurs during the 7th week.
• May involve the iris, ciliary body, retina, or optic nerve.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Explain the inductive relationship between the optic vesicle and the surface ectoderm during early eye formation.
back:
• Optic vesicle contacts surface ectoderm.
• This contact induces ectoderm to thicken into the lens placode.
• The lens placode then induces the optic vesicle to form the optic cup.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the embryological origins of the pupillary muscles (sphincter/dilator) with the ciliary muscle.
back:
• Pupillary muscles: Derived from neuroectoderm of the optic cup (unique ectodermal origin).
• Ciliary muscle: Derived from the surrounding mesenchyme (mesodermal origin).

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Identify the three embryological layers that contribute to the formation of the definitive cornea.
back:
• External epithelial layer: Surface ectoderm.
• Substantia propria (Stroma): Mesenchyme continuous with the sclera.
• Inner epithelial layer: Mesenchyme bordering the anterior chamber.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: The 'master gene' for eye development, which regulates the initial eye field and lens differentiation, is [___].
back:
• PAX6.
• Expressed in the anterior neural ridge.
• Mutations lead to aniridia (absence of iris) or microphthalmia.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: A child is born with bilateral opaque lenses after the mother contracted a viral infection in the first trimester. Name the condition and the embryological structures affected.
back:
• Congenital Cataracts (Rubella Syndrome).
• Affects primary lens fibers derived from the posterior wall of the lens vesicle.
• Most vulnerable between weeks 4 and 7.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Describe the formation of the anterior chamber and the fate of the iridopupillary membrane.
back:
• Formed by vacuolization within the mesenchyme between the lens and cornea.
• Mesenchyme splits into an inner iridopupillary membrane.
• This membrane normally disappears completely to allow light passage.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Distinguish between the mesenchymal origins of the sclera and the choroid.
back:
• Sclera: Derived from the outer mesenchymal layer (analogous to dura mater).
• Choroid: Derived from the inner, highly vascularized mesenchymal layer (analogous to pia mater).

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Which fetal vessel enters the optic cup via the choroid fissure to supply the lens and is later replaced by the central artery of the retina?
back:
• Hyaloid Artery.
• Distal part degenerates before birth.
• Failure to degenerate results in persistent hyaloid artery or cysts.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: During the 4th week of eye development, the [___] induces the overlying surface ectoderm to thicken and differentiate into the lens placode.
back:
● Optic vesicle
● Formed as an outpocketing of the forebrain
● Contact with surface ectoderm is essential for induction.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: A neonate presents with a keyhole-shaped defect in the inferior iris. Identify the embryological failure responsible for this presentation.
back:
● Failure of the choroid fissure to close
● Occurs during the 7th week of development
● May extend to ciliary body, retina, or optic nerve.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Explain the dual embryological origin of the ciliary body.
back:
● Neuroectoderm: Pars ciliaris retinae (inner layer)
● Mesenchyme: Ciliary muscle and connective tissue
● Function: Regulates lens curvature via suspensory ligaments.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the mesenchyme-derived layers that form the choroid versus the sclera.
back:
● Choroid: Inner, highly vascularized pigmented layer; analogous to pia mater.
● Sclera: Outer, fibrous protective layer; analogous to dura mater and continuous with it.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Identify the unique embryological origin of the sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles.
back:
● Derived from the neuroectoderm of the optic cup
● Rare example of muscle arising from ectoderm rather than mesoderm.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: The substantia propria (stroma) of the cornea is continuous with the [___] and is derived from mesenchyme.
back:
● Sclera
● The cornea also comprises surface ectoderm (epithelium) and neural crest (endothelium).

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: A child is born with an opaque lens following maternal infection during the 6th week of gestation. Explain the developmental pathophysiology.
back:
● Congenital Cataract
● Rubella virus disrupts lens fiber differentiation between weeks 4 and 7
● Primary lens fibers fail to fill the lens vesicle lumen properly.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Describe the mechanism by which the single eye field is separated into two optic primordia.
back:
● Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) from the prechordal plate
● Inhibits PAX6 in the midline
● Upregulates PAX2 in the optic stalks to divide the field.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Distinguish between primary and secondary lens fibers.
back:
● Primary: Elongation of posterior lens vesicle wall cells; fill the vesicle lumen by week 7.
● Secondary: Continuously added to the central core from the equatorial zone throughout life.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Identify the structure that normally disappears to form the anterior chamber but may persist as a web of connective tissue over the pupil.
back:
● Iridopupillary membrane
● Derived from mesenchyme in front of the lens and iris
● Persistent membrane rarely interferes with vision unless extensive.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: The [___] is the embryological precursor of the lens, formed by the thickening of surface ectoderm upon contact with the optic vesicle during the fourth week.
back:
• Lens placode
  • Invaginates to form the lens vesicle
  • Induces the optic vesicle to transform into the optic cup

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: A neonate presents with bilateral opaque lenses and sensorineural hearing loss. The mother reported a febrile rash during the first trimester. Identify the defect and the timing of the insult.
back:
• Diagnosis: Congenital Cataracts
  • Pathophysiology: Rubella virus infection
  • Timing: Between 4th and 7th weeks of gestation
  • Result: Interference with lens fiber differentiation from the lens vesicle

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Explain the unique histological origin of the sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles compared to other body muscles.
back:
• Origin: Neuroectoderm of the optic cup
  • Derived from the anterior rim of the optic cup (pars iridica retinae)
  • Contrast: Most other muscles originate from mesoderm/neural crest

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the embryological defect resulting in an iris coloboma with the persistence of the iridopupillary membrane.
back:
• Iris Coloboma: Failure of the choroid fissure to close in the 7th week (keyhole-shaped cleft).
  • Persistent Membrane: Failure of the mesenchyme in front of the lens to resorb during anterior chamber formation.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Identify the three distinct embryological sources that contribute to the formation of the adult cornea.
back:
• Surface ectoderm: Forms the anterior epithelium
  • Mesenchyme (neural crest/mesoderm): Forms the stroma (substantia propria)
  • Neural crest: Forms the posterior epithelial lining (endothelium)

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: The vascularized, pigmented layer of the eye known as the choroid is derived from the [___] layer of mesenchyme surrounding the optic cup.
back:
• Inner (Pia-like) layer
  • The outer layer forms the sclera (Dura-like)
  • The mesenchyme is derived from both neural crest and mesoderm

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: A child presents with a complete absence of the iris (aniridia). This condition is most commonly associated with a mutation in which master eye regulatory gene?
back:
• PAX6 gene
  • Role: Key transcription factor for eye development and optic cup rim induction
  • Clinical Note: May be associated with Wilms tumor in WAGR syndrome

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Describe the process by which the optic stalk is converted into the definitive optic nerve.
back:
• The choroid fissure closes in the 7th week, enclosing the hyaloid artery
  • Retinal nerve fibers grow through the inner wall of the stalk
  • The inner and outer layers of the stalk fuse to form the nerve structure

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the development of the primary lens fibers with the secondary lens fibers.
back:
• Primary fibers: Formed by elongation of cells from the posterior wall of the lens vesicle
  • Secondary fibers: Continuously added to the central core from the equatorial region during fetal life and after birth

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: List the derivatives of the anterior 1/5th of the inner layer of the optic cup (pars ceca retinae).
back:
• Pars iridica retinae: Inner layer of the iris
  • Pars ciliaris retinae: Contributes to the ciliary body epithelium
  • Both lack photoreceptive rods and cones

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: The internal ear first appears as a thickening of the surface ectoderm on each side of the rhombencephalon called the [___].
back:
• Otic placode.
• Appears at approximately 22 days.
• Invaginates to form the otic vesicle (otocyst).

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: A neonate is diagnosed with sensorineural hearing loss. Structural imaging shows a malformed spiral organ. Identify the embryological precursor of this structure.
back:
• Cochlear duct.
• Derived from the ventral component of the otic vesicle.
• Forms the spiral Organ of Corti for sound transduction.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Explain the process by which the scala vestibuli and scala tympani are formed from the surrounding mesenchyme.
back:
• Surrounding mesenchyme differentiates into a cartilaginous shell.
• In the 10th week, this shell undergoes vacuolization.
• Creates perilymphatic spaces surrounding the cochlear duct.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the embryological derivatives of the ventral versus dorsal components of the otic vesicle.
back:
• Ventral: Saccule and cochlear duct (Hearing).
• Dorsal: Utricle, semicircular canals, and endolymphatic duct (Equilibrium).

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Name the specific embryological structure that maintains the connection between the saccule and the cochlear duct.
back:
• Ductus reuniens.
• It is a narrow pathway resulting from the tubular outpocketing of the saccule.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: The central axis of the bony cochlea, derived from a cartilaginous process that supports the median angle of the cochlear duct, is the [___].
back:
• Modiolus.
• Forms the supporting core around which the cochlea completes its 2.5 turns.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: A pregnant woman contracts Rubella during her 8th week of gestation. Explain why the newborn is at risk for sensorineural deafness despite a potentially normal lens.
back:
• Rubella after the 7th week specifically targets the cochlear duct.
• Disrupts the differentiation of the spiral organ of Corti.
• Results in malformed hair cells or sensory neurons.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
coreConcept: Histogenesis of the Organ of Corti
front: Describe the histogenesis of the inner and outer hair cells from the epithelium of the cochlear duct.
back:
• Epithelial cells form an inner and outer ridge.
• The outer ridge differentiates into one inner row and 3-4 outer rows of hair cells.
• These are the sensory cells of the auditory system.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Differentiate between the development of the crista ampullaris and the maculae acusticae.
back:
• Crista ampullaris: Sensory areas in the ampullae of semicircular canals.
• Maculae acusticae: Sensory areas in the walls of the utricle and saccule.
• Both detect changes in equilibrium.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Identify the two distinct sources from which the cells of the statoacoustic (vestibulocochlear) ganglion originate.
back:
• Otic vesicle (otocyst) wall.
• Neural crest cells.
• These combine to form the sensory neurons of CN VIII.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: The primary embryonic structure that invaginates from surface ectoderm on each side of the rhombencephalon to form the internal ear is the [___].
back:
Otic placode (or Otocyst/Otic vesicle).

* Appears at day 22.
* Forms from surface ectoderm.
* Invaginates into mesenchyme.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: A neonate is born with sensorineural deafness. Maternal history reveals a febrile illness with a rash during the 7th week of pregnancy. Identify the most likely pathogen and the specific internal ear structure damaged.
back:
Rubella virus; Organ of Corti.

* Rubella infection in weeks 4–8.
* Disrupts cochlear duct differentiation.
* Results in permanent sensorineural loss.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Describe the morphogenetic process leading to the formation of the three semicircular canals from the utricular portion of the otocyst.
back:
* Flattened outpocketings emerge.
* Central walls appose and fuse.
* Fused central portions disappear.
* Peripheral parts persist as canals.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the embryonic derivatives of the ventral and dorsal components of the otic vesicle.
back:
* Ventral: Saccule and Cochlear duct (Hearing).
* Dorsal: Utricle, Semicircular canals, and Endolymphatic duct (Balance/Equilibrium).

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Explain the formation of the perilymphatic spaces (scala vestibuli and scala tympani) surrounding the cochlear duct.
back:
* Surrounding mesenchyme chondrifies.
* Cartilaginous shell undergoes vacuolization (10th week).
* Separated from duct by vestibular and basilar membranes.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: The narrow pathway that maintains the connection between the saccule and the developing cochlear duct is the [___].
back:
Ductus reuniens.

* Connects ventral components.
* Formed from saccular outpocketing.
* Essential for endolymph continuity.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: A child presents with congenital deafness. Imaging reveals the cochlea has only 1.5 turns instead of the normal 2.5. Name this anomaly and its embryological basis.
back:
Mondini Dysplasia.

* Failure of cochlear duct elongation.
* Arrested spiral growth (normal is 2.5 turns).
* Occurs during weeks 6–8.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Detail the cellular differentiation of the 'outer ridge' of the cochlear duct into the functional sensory unit of hearing.
back:
* Forms Organ of Corti.
* Differentiates into hair cells (1 inner, 3-4 outer rows).
* Develops tectorial membrane (fibrillar gelatinous substance).

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Distinguish between the crista ampullaris and the maculae acusticae based on their specific anatomical location in the internal ear.
back:
* Crista ampullaris: Located in the ampullae of the semicircular canals.
* Maculae acusticae: Located in the walls of the utricle and saccule.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Identify the specific embryonic day when the otic placode first appears as a thickening of the surface ectoderm.
back:
Approximately Day 22.

* First sign of ear development.
* Located beside the rhombencephalon.
* Invaginates shortly after appearance.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: The internal ear first appears as a thickening of surface ectoderm on each side of the rhombencephalon called the [___].
back:
• Otic placode
• Appears at approximately day 22
• Invaginates to form the otic vesicle (otocyst)

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: A neonate is born with congenital sensorineural deafness. Histology reveals failure of the neuroepithelial cells to differentiate into hair cells. Identify the specific embryonic structure involved.
back:
• Organ of Corti
• Derived from the outer ridge of the cochlear duct
• Transduces sound vibrations into electrical signals

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Explain the morphological mechanism that results in the formation of the three semicircular canals from the utricular outpocketing.
back:
• Central walls of the outpocketings appose each other
• These central portions undergo programmed disappearance
• Peripheral portions remain as three distinct canals

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the adult derivatives of the ventral and dorsal components of the otic vesicle (otocyst).
back:
• Ventral: Saccule and Cochlear duct (hearing)
• Dorsal: Utricle, Semicircular canals, and Endolymphatic duct (equilibrium)

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Identify the process by which the scala vestibuli and scala tympani are formed within the surrounding mesenchyme.
back:
• Vacuolization of the cartilaginous shell
• Occurs during the 10th week of development
• Creates two perilymphatic spaces around the cochlear duct

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Communication between the saccule and the cochlear duct is maintained through a narrow pathway known as the [___].
back:
• Ductus reuniens
• Persists after the cochlear duct completes its 2.5 spiral turns

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: A mother contracts Rubella during the 8th week of gestation. Contrast the likely ocular outcome with the likely auditory outcome in the fetus.
back:
• Ocular: Escape damage (cataracts usually occur before week 7)
• Auditory: High risk of congenital deafness due to cochlear damage

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
coreConcept: Histogenesis of the Organ of Corti
front: Describe the differentiation of the cochlear duct's epithelial ridges into the functional components of the Organ of Corti.
back:
• Inner ridge: Becomes the spiral limbus
• Outer ridge: Forms one inner row and 3–4 outer rows of hair cells
• Tectorial membrane: Fibrillar gelatinous substance covering hair cells

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Differentiate the embryonic tissue origins of the membranous labyrinth versus the bony labyrinth.
back:
• Membranous: Surface ectoderm (via the otic vesicle)
• Bony: Surrounding mesenchyme (which first forms a cartilaginous shell)

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
coreConcept: Origin of Cranial Nerve VIII Ganglia
front: Name the two specific cellular sources that contribute to the formation of the statoacoustic (vestibulocochlear) ganglion.
back:
• Otic vesicle wall cells
• Neural crest cells
• Ganglion later splits into cochlear and vestibular portions

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: The first indication of internal ear development appears around day 22 as a thickening of surface ectoderm on each side of the rhombencephalon called the [___].
back:
• Otic placode.
• Invaginates rapidly to form the otic vesicle (otocyst).
• Differentiates into the components of the membranous labyrinth.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: A neonate presents with sensorineural deafness. History reveals maternal rubella infection during the 8th week of pregnancy, though the infant's lenses are clear. Identify the specific internal ear structure likely damaged.
back:
• Organ of Corti (Spiral organ).
• Rubella infection after the 7th week targets differentiating hair cells.
• Contrast: Infection in weeks 4–7 typically results in cataracts.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Explain the role of vacuolization in the mesenchyme surrounding the cochlear duct during the 10th week of development.
back:
• It transforms the cartilaginous shell into two perilymphatic spaces.
• Forms the scala vestibuli and scala tympani.
• Leaves the cochlear duct (scala media) as the central compartment.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the embryonic derivatives of the ventral and dorsal components of the otic vesicle (otocyst).
back:
• Ventral: Saccule and Cochlear duct (hearing function).
• Dorsal: Utricle, Semicircular canals, and Endolymphatic duct (balance function).
• Collectively form the membranous labyrinth.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Name the narrow epithelial connection that persists between the saccule and the cochlear duct.
back:
• Ductus reuniens.
• Maintains continuity between the saccular part and the spiral hearing apparatus.
• Formed as the cochlear duct grows from the lower pole of the saccule.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: The sensory areas developed within the ampullae of the semicircular canals, responsible for angular equilibrium, are the [___].
back:
• Crista ampullaris.
• Contain hair cells that transmit impulses to the vestibular fibers of CN VIII.
• Contrast: Maculae acusticae are the equivalent sensory areas in the utricle and saccule.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: A newborn is diagnosed with conductive hearing loss due to stapes fixation (ankylosis). Identify the specific embryological cell population whose defective signaling prevents proper development of the stapes footplate and oval window.
back:
• Neural crest cells.
• These cells direct the formation of the footplate and oval window.
• Without crest signals, the stapes cannot move (ankylosis).

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Describe the differentiation of the 'outer ridge' of the cochlear duct epithelium into the sensory components of hearing.
back:
• Differentiates into the inner hair cells (one row).
• Differentiates into the outer hair cells (three or four rows).
• These cells, with the tectorial membrane, form the Organ of Corti.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Distinguish between the tissue origins of the membranous labyrinth versus the bony labyrinth of the internal ear.
back:
• Membranous: Derived from surface ectoderm (otic vesicle).
• Bony: Derived from surrounding mesenchyme that chondrifies and later ossifies.
• The spaces between them (perilymphatic) form via vacuolization.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Identify the number of turns the cochlear duct must complete through the surrounding mesenchyme to be fully formed by the end of the 8th week.
back:
• 2.5 turns.
• Process starts in the 6th week and completes by the end of the 8th week.
• The central axis of this spiral is the cartilaginous modiolus.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: The primary embryological precursor of the lens is the [___], a thickening of surface ectoderm induced by contact with the optic vesicle.
back: • Lens placode. • Formed from surface ectoderm during the 4th week. • Invaginates to become the lens vesicle by the 5th week.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: A neonate presents with a keyhole-shaped defect in the inferior iris. This condition, coloboma iridis, results from the failure of the [___] to close properly.
back: • Choroid fissure (Optic fissure). • Normally closes during the 7th week of development. • Defect may extend to the ciliary body or retina.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Explain the unique embryological origin of the sphincter pupillae and dilator pupillae muscles.
back: • Derived from the neuroectoderm of the optic cup. • These are rare examples of muscles originating from ectoderm instead of mesoderm. • Located within the mesenchymal iris stroma.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the developmental origins of the three primary layers of the cornea.
back: • Outer epithelium: Surface ectoderm. • Substantia propria (Stroma): Mesenchyme continuous with the sclera. • Inner epithelium: Mesenchyme bordering the anterior chamber.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Aniridia, or the total absence of the iris, is most commonly associated with mutations in which master regulatory gene?
back: • PAX6. • This gene is essential for eye field separation and lens induction. • Mutations also cause microphthalmia and congenital cataracts.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: The [___] is a mesenchymal layer that temporarily covers the lens anteriorly but normally disappears to form the pupil.
back: • Iridopupillary membrane. • Forms during the creation of the anterior chamber. • Persistence results in congenital spider-web-like pupillary obstructions.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: A newborn presents with opaque, milky-white lenses. The mother reported a febrile illness with a rash during her first trimester. Identify the likely teratogen.
back: • Rubella virus (German Measles). • Causes congenital cataracts by interfering with primary lens fiber formation. • Critical period is between the 4th and 7th weeks.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Describe the mechanism by which the ciliary body enables lens accommodation.
back: • Pars ciliaris retinae and mesenchyme form ciliary processes. • Suspensory ligaments (zonule) connect these to the lens. • Ciliary muscle contraction reduces ligament tension, increasing lens curvature.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Distinguish between the mesenchymal analogues of the choroid and the sclera relative to the meninges.
back: • Choroid: Inner vascular layer, analogous to the pia mater. • Sclera: Outer fibrous layer, analogous to the dura mater. • Both derive from mesenchyme surrounding the optic cup.

category: Describe the development of cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, ciliary body and lens and relate it to their respective congenital anomalies
front: Which embryonic vessel passes through the choroid fissure to supply the developing lens before obliterating?
back: • Hyaloid artery. • The distal part degenerates during fetal life. • The proximal part persists as the central artery of the retina.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: The internal ear originates as a thickening of surface ectoderm known as the [___] on each side of the rhombencephalon.
back:
Otic placode.

*   Appears at approximately day 22.
*   Invaginates to form the otic vesicle (otocyst).
*   Eventually differentiates into the membranous labyrinth.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
coreConcept: Congenital Rubella Syndrome and Hearing Loss
front: A mother contracts Rubella in her 6th week of pregnancy. Explain the resulting embryological defect in the neonate's internal ear.
back:
Sensorineural deafness.

*   Rubella damages the differentiating hair cells in the Organ of Corti.
*   This window (4th–7th weeks) is the critical period for cochlear development.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Explain the 10th-week formation of the scala vestibuli and scala tympani from the cartilaginous otic capsule.
back:
Vacuolization of the cartilaginous shell.

*   Creates two perilymphatic spaces surrounding the cochlear duct.
*   Spaces are separated from the duct by vestibular and basilar membranes.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the developmental fates of the ventral and dorsal components of the otic vesicle.
back:
Ventral Component:
*   Gives rise to the saccule and the cochlear duct.
Dorsal Component:
*   Forms the utricle, semicircular canals, and endolymphatic duct.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Describe the inductive signaling 'step' from the hindbrain required to initiate internal ear development.
back:
Induction by the Rhombencephalon.

*   Signals from the hindbrain trigger the overlying surface ectoderm.
*   Results in the formation of the otic placode on day 22.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: The cochlear duct maintains its connection to the saccule via a narrow channel called the [___].
back:
Ductus reuniens.

*   Forms during the expansion of the saccule into the cochlear duct.
*   Ensures continuity within the membranous labyrinth system.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: A child has malformed semicircular canals. Trace this defect to the specific morphogenetic failure in the utricular outpocketings.
back:
Failure of central wall apposition.

*   Walls of utricular outpocketings must appose, fuse, and disappear.
*   Failure prevents the formation of three distinct, circular canals.

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Differentiate the embryological basis of sensorineural hearing loss from conductive hearing loss caused by meatal plug persistence.
back:
Sensorineural:
*   Failure of Organ of Corti hair cells or auditory nerve (internal ear).
Conductive:
*   Failure of the 1st arch meatal plug to canalize (external ear).

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Contrast the fluids found within the membranous labyrinth versus the scala vestibuli.
back:
Endolymph:
*   Located inside the membranous labyrinth (otic vesicle origin).
Perilymph:
*   Located in the scalae (formed by mesenchymal vacuolization).

category: Describe the development of internal ear and give the embryological basis of associated congenital anomalies
front: Identify the number of turns the cochlear duct completes by the end of the eighth week of gestation.
back:
2.5 turns.

*   Begins as a tubular outgrowth in the 6th week.
*   Penetrates the surrounding mesenchyme in a spiral fashion.
